metadata.title: The role of item format in the PISA 2018 mathematics literacy assessment: A cross-country study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 computer-based assessment (CBA) mathematics item response data from 71 countries/economies, restricting to students who received mathematics clusters. The paper describes PISA’s sampling targets (about 5,000–6,000 students per country) and the rotated-booklet design, but it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the cross-classified mixed-effects estimation. The models are estimated separately within each country using full information maximum likelihood in R (lme4), followed by multivariate random-effects meta-analysis across countries; this workflow is not presented as a complex-survey-weighted analysis. Because no weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate schemes (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are mentioned, weighting is treated as not reported for the analytic models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary-scored correctness indicator for individual PISA mathematics items (correct vs incorrect), modeled with cross-classified mixed-effects logistic models. Plausible values are typically used for cognitive achievement scales, but this paper models item-level response probabilities directly rather than PV-based achievement scores, so PV handling is not applicable. Missing-data handling is not described for the item-response modeling; while the gender questionnaire item is stated to have no missingness due to cross-referencing, the paper does not document how any missingness in item responses or other covariates (if present) was handled, which is a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 mathematics literacy item response data only from countries/economies that administered the computer-based assessment (CBA) version (71 countries/economies). Further restricted to students who received a booklet containing mathematics items (i.e., eligible for the mathematics clusters). Students were included regardless of whether they received MC or CR items, but item responses were modeled at the item level with binary scoring (partially credited items recoded as incorrect). Countries that administered the alternative simplified mathematics cluster version (M6B) were retained to preserve sample size.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics literacy (CBA), item-level responses (rotated booklet; 71 countries/economies)
main_findings.target_variable: Probability of correct response to a mathematics item (binary correctness)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cross-country multivariate random-effects meta-analysis (logit scale): item format effect b1 = −1.13 (95% CI [−1.21, −1.05]); prediction interval [−1.51, −0.75]. Average probabilities: 48% correct for MC vs 23% for CR. Variance reduction: item format explained 12% of item variance on average (R2(β̂i) > 0 in all countries except Singapore).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics literacy (CBA) item-level response data across 71 countries/economies, the study leveraged item format (MC vs CR) and gender to model the probability of correct responses to individual mathematics items, finding that constructed response (CR) items were consistently more difficult than multiple-choice (MC) items (b1 = −1.13; average 48% vs 23% correct). This indicates that item format is a construct-irrelevant difficulty determinant that can bias cross-country comparisons of mathematics performance, especially when secondary analyses treat item difficulties as format-neutral.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics literacy (CBA), item-level responses (rotated booklet; 71 countries/economies)
main_findings.target_variable: Cross-country variation in item format effect (MC vs CR) by gender
main_findings.performance_metrics: Interaction model meta-analysis (logit scale): interaction term b12 = −0.09 (95% CI [−0.11, −0.07]); prediction interval [−0.21, 0.03]. Converted to probabilities: average male MC–CR difference 26% (50% vs 24%, OR = 3.17) vs average female difference 23% (46% vs 23%, OR = 2.85). Country-level interaction direction consistent in most countries; overall moderating effect small (none exceeding 5% absolute probability difference).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics literacy (CBA) item-level response data across 71 countries/economies, the study leveraged item format (MC vs CR), gender, and their interaction to examine whether the MC–CR difficulty gap differs by gender within countries, finding a small but consistent negative interaction (b12 = −0.09) with probability differences of about 23–26% for males vs females of equal mathematics ability. This indicates that gender-related fairness concerns from item format are present but limited in magnitude, while cross-country differences in format effects remain the more substantial threat to comparability.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 mathematics literacy CBA item responses from students who received mathematics booklets in 71 countries/economies (total sample over 260,000). Using cross-classified mixed-effects logistic models estimated separately per country and then pooled via multivariate random-effects meta-analysis, it models item-level correctness as a function of item format (MC vs CR) and gender, including an interaction. Across countries, CR items were more difficult than MC items: the pooled logit effect was b1 = −1.13 (95% CI [−1.21, −1.05]) with average correct-response probabilities of 23% (CR) vs 48% (MC). Item format explained 12% of item variance on average, but the effect varied by country (larger in lower-performing systems). The gender moderation was small (interaction b12 = −0.09), suggesting limited within-country fairness impact. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weighting and missing-data handling for item responses, and the fact that the analysis targets item difficulty rather than PV-based achievement.
